source_spans.locator: PNAS 88(11), published p.4966, Abstract and opening: repeated practice produces durable improvement in a masked texture-discrimination task; the paper asks what level of visual processing can account for the learned improvement

PNAS 88(11), published pp.4966-4967, task/method description: peripheral three-element target embedded in a line-texture background, central letter task used to enforce fixation, target followed by a patterned mask, and performance measured as the target-to-mask interval required for reliable discrimination

PNAS 88(11), published pp.4967-4968, practice and location-transfer results: the trained retinal location shows large threshold improvement; moving the target to an untrained retinal location substantially removes the acquired advantage and renewed practice can improve the new location

PNAS 88(11), published pp.4968-4969, eye-transfer results: training performed monocularly shows little transfer when testing is switched to the untrained eye, demonstrating strong eye specificity under the reported training procedure

PNAS 88(11), published pp.4968-4969, orientation-transfer results: improvement is specific to the trained background-element orientation, while changing the target-element orientation produces substantial transfer; orientation specificity is therefore asymmetric across stimulus components

PNAS 88(11), published pp.4969-4970, interpretation/discussion: the joint retinotopic, monocular, and background-orientation specificity is used to infer experience-dependent change at an early visual-processing level preserving eye, retinal-location, and orientation organization; primary visual cortex localization is presented as an interpretation, not as a direct neural measurement

provenance.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

conditions: repeated practice on a briefly presented, backward-masked texture-discrimination task
post-practice testing varies retinal location, viewing eye, background-element orientation, or target-element orientation relative to training
task: discriminate whether a peripheral array of three oriented elements forms a horizontal or vertical target within an oriented background while maintaining central fixation
temporal_scope: performance across repeated practice sessions and subsequent transfer tests
durable improvement retained beyond the immediately practiced trials

nodes.description: repeated performance of the masked peripheral texture-discrimination task under a fixed training configuration
time from target-display onset to mask onset, varied to control discrimination difficulty
target-to-mask interval required to maintain reliable target-orientation discrimination, with lower threshold indicating improved performance
central letter-discrimination task used to maintain fixation while the peripheral target is tested
post-practice testing that changes one training dimension to measure how much of the acquired performance advantage transfers
whether the tested target occupies the retinal location used during practice or an untrained retinal location
whether testing uses the eye exposed during monocular practice or the previously untrained eye
whether the test background elements retain the orientation experienced during practice or are changed to another orientation
whether the local orientation of the target elements matches the practiced target-element orientation
amount of the practice-related threshold improvement expressed under a transfer-test condition

source-authored interpretation that the observed specificity pattern reflects experience-dependent change at an early visual-processing level that still preserves retinal position, eye-of-origin, and orientation organization

relations.description: repeated practice lowers the target-to-mask interval required for reliable discrimination in the trained configuration
testing altered versions of the trained configuration measures how much of the acquired threshold improvement is retained
the acquired advantage is strongly local to the practiced retinal position and is substantially lost when testing moves to an untrained location
the acquired advantage is strongly tied to the practiced eye, with little transfer to the previously untrained eye under the reported procedure
changing the orientation of the background elements greatly reduces the learned advantage
unlike background orientation, target-element orientation is not strongly specific: substantial transfer is retained when target-element orientation is changed
orientation specificity is asymmetric across stimulus components: transfer depends strongly on background orientation but not comparably on target-element orientation

the conjunction of retinotopic, eye, and background-orientation specificity is used by the authors to infer an early visually organized locus of experience-dependent change; the behavioral data do not directly measure a cortical site
